definition: Separating a mixture of overlapping speech signals into individual speaker streams — the “cocktail party problem.” Modern systems use deep networks such as Conv-TasNet and are a front end for transcription and diarization.
details: Separating a mixture of overlapping speech signals into individual speaker streams — the “cocktail party problem.” Modern systems use deep networks such as Conv-TasNet and are a front end for transcription and diarization.

explainer.lead: Speech separation splits a mixture of overlapping speech signals into individual speaker streams, known as the cocktail party problem. It serves as a front end for transcription and diarization, making overlapping audio usable downstream.

tiers.eli5: Imagine several people talking at once at a party; this is the technology that pulls each voice out of the jumble.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers place it as a front end before transcription and diarization so downstream models receive clean per-speaker streams. Modern systems use deep networks such as Conv-TasNet.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined as separating a mixture of overlapping speech signals into individual speaker streams, the cocktail party problem; deep networks such as Conv-TasNet are the modern approach. No formula or numerical performance limit is given.

explainer.example: Two people speak at once into a single microphone; a Conv-TasNet-based system outputs two separated streams, one per speaker.
